claims.text: The relatively low hardness and strength, together with favorable plasticity, of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi primarily result from its processing-dependent microstructure.
The relevant microstructure is a non-equilibrium nanocrystalline solid solution.
Severe lattice strain and high dislocation density from high-energy ball milling, followed by rapid SPS densification, stabilize a mixed FCC/BCC structure.
The starting and processed alloy is nominally equimolar CoCrFeNiTi, corresponding to approximately Co20Cr20Fe20Ni20Ti20 in atomic percent.
High-energy ball milling for 1–6 hours induces significant lattice strain and nanocrystallinity in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
Rapid diffusion and densification during SPS promote a uniform microstructure with limited porosity.
The processed alloy will have grain sizes below 48 nm.
The processed alloy will contain approximately 83% FCC and 17% BCC phases.
Nanometer-scale grains increase hardness and compressive strength through Hall–Petch grain-boundary strengthening.
Dislocation accumulation caused by aggressive milling contributes to strengthening.
Atomic-size mismatch, particularly that associated with Ti, provides solid-solution strengthening.
The mixed FCC/BCC structure balances ductility and strength.
Conventionally cast CoCrFeNiTi alloys suffer from porosity and microstructural heterogeneity.
The HEBM-plus-SPS alloy will attain a density greater than 6.5 g/cm³.
The HEBM-plus-SPS alloy will attain a Vickers hardness of approximately 675 HV.
The HEBM-plus-SPS alloy will attain a compressive strength near 1894 MPa.
The processed alloy will display predominantly intergranular fracture features associated with high strength but modest ductility.
Cast equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has hardness below 675 HV and lower compressive strength than the HEBM-plus-SPS alloy.
SPS at 900–1000 °C achieves maximum densification without grain coarsening.
Milling for 1–6 hours supplies sufficient strain and nanocrystallinity without causing deleterious phase transformations or excessive aggregation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis identifies the milled, nanocrystalline mixed-phase microstructure as the primary cause of relatively low hardness and strength, but the mechanism and prediction say that this same microstructure enhances hardness and strength to about 675 HV and 1894 MPa relative to the cast baseline.

The target property combination includes favorable plasticity, whereas the predicted processed material is described as having modest ductility and predominantly intergranular fracture. The relationship between these deformation descriptions is not reconciled.
